strengths: Addresses practically important problem: Quantifying noise robustness of Wasserstein metrics is well-motivated by cryo-EM applications where empirical evidence suggests Wasserstein metrics outperform L2

Solid theoretical contributions: Non-asymptotic bounds with explicit dependence on image size n, noise level σ, and Wasserstein order p. Distinguishes scaling regimes (p=1 vs p>1) showing fundamental differences
Clever noise model design: Zero-sum Gaussian assumption (Assumption 1) elegantly avoids rescaling complications while remaining analytically tractable, with clear characterization in Proposition 2

Comprehensive experimental validation: Figure 2 shows good empirical agreement with theory; multiple image classes tested; Figure 6 demonstrates W2 preserves geometric structure better than L2 in cryo-EM setting
Clear presentation and rigor: Well-organized exposition, correct use of dyadic partitions and Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality, complete proofs in appendix
Novel empirical phenomenon: Discovery and mechanistic explanation of how noise can decrease Wasserstein distance in sparse configurations, with visualized transport maps
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Core technique directly applies Weed & Bach (2019) dyadic partition bounds to new setting without substantial methodological innovation. Extension to signed measures uses existing Mainini (2012) construction. For ICML standards, contribution feels incremental

Significant theory-practice gap: Bounds contain multiple loose √2 factors; Figure 3 shows W2 and W3 bounds substantially exceed empirical values; log²(n) factor in Theorem 4 not observed empirically. Only lower bound provided for p=1, single-image case. Authors acknowledge but don't resolve

Restrictive noise model: Zero-sum Gaussian (Assumption 1) is convenient but potentially unrealistic; real cryo-EM noise may differ. No robustness analysis to model misspecification. Standard i.i.d. noise only briefly mentioned in Section 3.2, not analyzed. Generalization to other noise distributions unexplored

Incomplete two-image analysis: Theorem 5 (most practically relevant case) provides complex bound mixing W₁(μ,ν)^(1/p) and noise terms without clear intuition for when each dominates. Theorem 4's additive √2/n term is unexplained and seems odd dimensionally

Non-metric property of signed Wasserstein for p>1: Lacks triangle inequality (acknowledged), limiting applicability. This explains decreasing distance phenomenon but systematic characterization missing. Theorem 5's complexity may partially result from this structural issue

Limited experimental scope: Mostly 32×32 images; scalability unclear. Cryo-EM application (Section 4.3) qualitative rather than quantitative; geometric preservation could be measured more rigorously. No comparison with unbalanced OT variants or other robust metrics

Incomplete reproducibility: Github link incomplete; OT solver configuration not specified (which algorithm from POT package?); sampling procedure for DOTMark images unclear. Only 100 trials; no confidence intervals provided

Missing lower bounds and tightness analysis: Except for Theorem 2 (p=1, single image), no lower bounds. Tightness of results Theorems 3-5 unclear. Makes it difficult to assess whether bounds capture fundamental limits or are artifacts of proof technique

strengths: First systematic theoretical analysis of Wasserstein metric noise sensitivity for images with non-asymptotic bounds
Clear theoretical scaling results (p-Wasserstein error scales as (nσ)^(1/p) vs. L2's linear scaling)
Technically sound proofs leveraging Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality and dyadic decomposition
Comprehensive experimental validation on synthetic, microscopy, and cryo-EM images
Well-written with complete proofs; honest discussion of limitations including loose bounds for p>1
weaknesses: Restrictive assumptions (zero-sum noise, cyclic boundaries, signed measures) limit practical applicability and generalization to standard i.i.d. noise scenarios
Significant theory-practice gap: bounds are loose, especially for p>1 (Figure 3); no lower bounds for Theorems 3-5 to establish optimality
Unexplained contradictions: 'decreasing distance phenomenon' (Section 4.4, Figures 4, 7) directly contradicts noise robustness narrative; lacks theoretical characterization of when distances decrease
Signed Wasserstein metric lacks triangle inequality for p>1, weakening theoretical guarantees and limiting applicability to learning/clustering tasks

Limited novelty and scope: primary contribution is applying existing techniques (Weed & Bach 2019 dyadic bounds, KR duality) to bound noise effects; specialized for OT community rather than broader ICML audience
Key result ('W2 more robust than L2') was already known empirically; practical guidance limited when bounds cannot predict behavior accurately
Missing code repository link for reproducibility; experiment-theory disconnect (theory for arbitrary n, experiments only on 32×32)
Artificial problem formulation: introducing signed measures only because pixel-wise noise can create negative values feels like working around a limitation rather than solving the core problem

strengths: Addresses important, previously understudied problem with clear motivation from cryo-EM and generative modeling applications
Solid theoretical contributions with rigorous proofs covering multiple practical settings (single image, two images, different p values)
Clever zero-sum noise model (Assumption 1) that elegantly avoids rescaling complications while maintaining realism
Theoretical predictions match empirical behavior: Figure 2 confirms (nσ)^(1/p) scaling for W₂ with measured exponent ~0.5
Interesting discovery and clear explanation of counter-intuitive decreasing-distance phenomenon for sparse images
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple image types (microscopy, cryo-EM, synthetic) with 100-trial averaging and exact transport costs
Cryo-EM case study (Figure 6) compellingly demonstrates practical relevance: W₂ preserves geometric structure where L² fails
Well-structured presentation with logical flow from motivation to theory to experiments; clear figures and honest limitations discussion
Complete and detailed proofs; rigorous use of appropriate mathematical techniques (KR duality, dyadic bounds, multiscale analysis)
weaknesses: Bounds are loose and gaps not fully explained: Figure 3 shows substantial discrepancy between theory and empirical distances, particularly for W₂ and W₃; no discussion of whether (nσ)^(1/p) scaling is optimal
Limited practical algorithmic impact: paper provides theoretical understanding but no methods to improve applications like cryo-EM; unclear how practitioners should use these bounds

Restricted problem setting reduces generalizability: requires discrete gridded images with cyclic boundary conditions, power-of-2 dimensions, unit grid spacing; unclear how results extend to continuous settings or realistic image dimensions
Code availability compromised: promised GitHub link is placeholder ('Github Repo') with no actual URL, limiting reproducibility despite detailed proofs
Zero-sum noise model, while motivated, differs from realistic pixel-wise additive noise; impact of this modeling choice on practical relevance unexplored; no experiments with alternative noise models
Theorem 1's bound depends on 1/∑Sμε,νε(x) which can explode for sparse noisy images; limited discussion of when this result is applicable
Missing comparisons: partial/unbalanced OT mentioned but not compared experimentally; no comparison to other robustness frameworks or competing distance metrics
Incomplete experimental analysis: no ablation studies on Assumption 1, W₂ non-monotonicity ('dips') in Figure 4 mostly unexplained, limited error analysis under assumption violations
Logarithmic factors (log₂ n) in Theorems 2 and 4 not analyzed: unclear if they are proof artifacts or fundamental
Technical presentation issues: signed Wasserstein definition introduced multiple times, cyclic boundary condition detail placed late in paper, some dense theorem statements

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First rigorous analysis of Wasserstein metric noise robustness for pixel-grid measures with additive Gaussian noise
Comprehensive theoretical results: Multiple theorems (3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 3.8) covering different scenarios with clear demonstration of (nσ)^(1/p) scaling advantage over L² metric
Clever technical approach: Zero-sum noise model elegantly avoids rescaling issues; sophisticated dyadic decomposition and multiscale analysis correctly applied

Well-designed experiments: Quantitative validation of scaling laws (Fig. 2), meaningful cryo-EM case study (Section 4.3) showing W₂ preserves geometry while L² fails, interesting discovery of non-monotonic distance phenomenon (Section 4.4)
Rigorous proofs: Detailed mathematical exposition with carefully constructed lower bounds via Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality; complete proofs in appendices verifiable and sound
Clear presentation and honesty: Well-motivated introduction, good organization, informative visualizations, transparent acknowledgment of gaps between bounds and limitations of noise model
weaknesses: Significant gaps between bounds: For p=1, upper bound O(nσ log n) vs lower bound Θ(nσ); for p>1, additional asymptotic gaps in n-dependence. While acknowledged, these reduce practical utility and suggest bounds may be loose

Limited scope of noise model: Analysis restricted to zero-sum Gaussian noise; no treatment of Poisson, multiplicative, or other noise types; cyclic boundary conditions may not reflect realistic images

Unclear practical utility: Complex bound expressions (e.g., Theorem 3.7) lack guidance for practitioners; no discussion of how to use bounds for parameter selection or algorithm design in applications

Insufficient analysis of non-monotonic phenomenon: Section 4.4's observation that distance can decrease with increasing noise is interesting but incompletely explained; intuition provided (Fig. 9) but lacks rigorous characterization of when/why this occurs
Missing code release: Reproducibility statement references code URL that is not provided; while proofs are detailed, public code would strengthen reproducibility claim

Limited experimental scope: Most experiments on 32×32 images without investigating scaling to realistic sizes; no computational cost analysis; no comparison to alternative approaches or robustness metrics
Assumption constraints not fully discussed: Several theorems assume n=2^η for convenience; results specific to unit grid with cyclic topology; unclear how bounds change for other settings

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First systematic theoretical study of Wasserstein metric noise robustness on fixed pixel grids
Rigorous theoretical framework: Multiple theorems with both upper and lower bounds; clever noise model avoiding mass rescaling
Interesting empirical findings: Decreasing distance phenomenon is well-explained and non-obvious
Relevant application domain: Cryo-EM is a genuine high-noise setting where theory could have impact
weaknesses: Unrealistic noise model: Assumption 3.2 (zero-sum correlated Gaussian) chosen for analytical convenience, not practical relevance. Real imaging noise differs significantly. Restrictive structure severely limits applicability.
Admittedly loose bounds: Authors acknowledge bounds are not tight (p. 8). Significant gaps between upper/lower bounds, especially for p > 1. No intuition provided for looseness or path to tightening.
Incomplete theory for p > 1: W±_p is not a metric for p > 1 (lacks triangle inequality). Theorem 3.8 less clean than p=1 case. Contradicts claims of improved robustness with higher p.

Severe theory-practice gap: Experiments only on 32×32 synthetic images with artificial noise; no comparison to real cryo-EM methods; cyclic boundary conditions not realistic; cryo-EM case study uses artificial normalization and evaluates only distance matrix preservation, not reconstruction performance.

Limited proof technique novelty: Proofs rely almost entirely on standard dyadic partition bounds from Weed & Bach (2019); lower bounds use elementary indicator functions; no deep structural insights into OT under noise.
Practical guidance absent: No recommendations on which Wasserstein metric to use, at what noise levels bounds are meaningful, or how results relate to downstream task performance.

strengths: Novel first study of noise robustness for Wasserstein metrics on fixed pixel grids with rigorous theoretical analysis
Sound mathematical framework with complete proofs using multiscale dyadic partitioning arguments
Practical motivation well-established through cryo-EM applications where empirical success of OT metrics needs theoretical justification
Main result (error scales as σ^(1/p) vs linear for L₂) is significant and has clear practical implications
Comprehensive experimental validation with excellent agreement between theory and empirics (Figures 1-2)
Compelling cryo-EM case study demonstrating that W₂ preserves geometric structure when L₂ completely fails in high noise
Clever noise model (Assumption 3.2) elegantly avoids rescaling issues while remaining interpretable
Clear presentation with well-organized flow from motivation through theory to experiments
Honest treatment of limitations including gaps between bounds and tightness issues
Interesting discovery and explanation of the decreasing distance phenomenon
weaknesses: Gaps between upper and lower bounds, particularly for p>1 (e.g., O(√n) gap for p=2)
Restrictive noise model requiring perfectly correlated zero-sum Gaussian noise, which may not match real imaging noise with spatial correlation
Limited scope: results apply only to fixed grids, not point clouds with corrupted locations
Bounds are tight only in worst-case scenarios and appear loose for realistic intermediate configurations (acknowledged in Section 4.2)
Lack of finite-sample high-probability bounds; only expectation bounds provided
Signed Wasserstein distance lacks triangle inequality for p>1, limiting theoretical results and creating fundamental analysis constraints
Limited practical guidance for practitioners on when to use Wasserstein metrics beyond qualitative understanding
Limited practical utility of bounds for specific applications due to looseness and worst-case nature
Paper is quite dense (18 pages + appendix) and could benefit from condensing some material
